subtitle: How Docker uses Linux cgroups to bound what a container can consume

panels.title: CPU and memory limits in practice
panels.body:
# Hard memory limit — OOM kill if exceeded
docker run -m 512m myapp

# Memory + swap: 512MB RAM + 256MB swap (total 768MB)
docker run -m 512m --memory-swap 768m myapp

# No swap access
docker run -m 512m --memory-swap 512m myapp

# CPU: 1.5 cores worth of CPU time
docker run --cpus 1.5 myapp

# Pin to specific CPU cores
docker run --cpuset-cpus "0,2" myapp

# Soft CPU weight (only matters under contention)
docker run --cpu-shares 512 myapp   # half weight of default (1024)

# Fork-bomb protection
docker run --pids-limit 200 myapp

panels.title: Critical memory gotchas
panels.body:
free / top inside a container show HOST memory, not container limits.
This is a longstanding Linux cgroup quirk — the /proc filesystem
reports host-wide values. Tools like 'free' are misleading inside containers.
Use: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max to see the actual limit.

--oom-kill-disable WITHOUT -m set → host can run out of memory.
Only use --oom-kill-disable when -m is also set.

Docker daemon has a lower OOM score than containers.
Under memory pressure, kernel kills containers before the daemon.

panels.title: --memory-swap semantics
pros: --memory-swap=-1: unlimited swap; container can use all host swap — good for bursty workloads
Unset --memory-swap with -m set: container gets equal swap to RAM (e.g. -m 512m → 512MB swap)
cons: --memory-swap equal to --memory: zero swap access; OOM kill happens at RAM limit with no grace period
Swap adds latency; database containers should set --memory-swap equal to --memory to force OOM over swap thrash
